title: Dynamics of Sheath Subunit of a Contractile Injection System Studied at Atomic Level During Host Infection
content: The sheath of a Tail Baseplate (TB) complex belonging to a Contractile Injection Systems (CISs) like P1 myophage suffers a nonuniform compression during the infection process that drives a non-contractile tail tube downwards, in a corkscrew manner, inside the host cytoplasm delivering the designated cargo. Studies have established that the sheath gradually translates from the normal to a compressed state, transitioning from one helical pattern to an entirely different one [1]. The noteworthy fact here is the structural integrity of the sheath molecules that always preserves a 6-fold point group symmetry (perpendicular to the helical axis of the tube) and maintains the interaction between subunits belonging to the upper and lower slabs by maintaining the handshake unit [2,3]. These studies have suggested that during the compression that each of the sheath subunits undergo a gyrating motion, as a single entity, moving away from the helical axis, thus expanding the diameter, and constricting the length sheath tube. Intermediates of such molecular rearrangement have not been investigated extensively until recently when studies on the non-uniform state of sheath tube of T4 and pyocin were published, which primarily focused on the energetics involved in the molecular re-arrangement [4,5].
